---
title: "Cardiac Muscle"
subtitle: "How the myocyte's structure and Ca^2+^ handling make the heart a pump"
---

::: {.callout-note title="Goals for this chapter"}
- Describe the structure of cardiac muscle, from the layers of the heart wall to the myocyte, and how it differs from skeletal muscle: branched cells, intercalated discs, dyads, many mitochondria.
- Explain what each part of the intercalated disc does: gap junctions, adherens junctions and desmosomes.
- Outline the conduction system, and contrast the action potential of a pacemaker cell with that of a ventricular myocyte.
- List the steps of cardiac excitation-contraction coupling, from the L-type Ca^2+^ channel through Ca^2+^-induced Ca^2+^ release to relaxation, and say where the Ca^2+^ goes.
- Explain how SERCA and phospholamban set the size of the next beat, and how epinephrine and norepinephrine use them to raise contractility.
- Explain the length-tension relationship of cardiac muscle and the Frank-Starling mechanism, and keep stretch separate from contractility.

Names, dates and the exact values in figure captions are context, not things to memorize.
:::

Cardiac output is the blood the heart pumps each minute. Along with heart rate, three things set it, and the three muscle types map onto them. The volume that fills the ventricle before it contracts (venous return, which sets end-diastolic volume) depends partly on skeletal muscle, whose pump squeezes blood back toward the heart. Vascular tone, which sets systemic vascular resistance (SVR), is the work of smooth muscle. And the strength of each beat depends on cardiac muscle. This chapter is about that third piece: how a cardiac myocyte is built, how an action potential becomes a contraction, and what lets the force of that contraction change from beat to beat.

The workload is large. At 70 beats per minute, the heart beats about 100,800 times a day, almost 37 million times a year, and about 2.8 billion times in a 75-year life. At a cardiac output of 5 L/min it pumps 7,200 L a day, close to 200 million liters in a lifetime: roughly 80 Olympic swimming pools. Most of the myocytes that do that work are the ones you were born with, because adult cardiac myocytes essentially do not divide.

This chapter builds on the sarcomere, the cross-bridge cycle and troponin regulation in [Skeletal Muscle](skeletal-muscle.qmd), and on the membrane potential in [Membrane Potentials and Excitable Cells](excitable-cells.qmd).

::: {.callout-note title="If you are comparing with the slides"}
The introduction slide lists the heart's contribution to cardiac output as "Contractility (Rate, inotropy, lusitropy)." In this course *contractility* means inotropy only: the intrinsic ability of the heart muscle to develop force at a given preload and afterload. It does not depend on loading. On the pressure-volume loop, greater contractility makes the end-systolic pressure-volume relationship steeper. Heart rate (chronotropy) and the speed of relaxation (lusitropy) are separate properties. All three affect cardiac output, but rate and relaxation are not part of contractility. This is errata entry 2.
:::

## Structure

### The heart wall

The heart wall has three layers. The outermost is the **epicardium**, which is the visceral layer of the pericardium. Outside it is the pericardial space, then the parietal pericardium and the tough fibrous pericardium, which anchors the heart in the chest. The middle layer, the **myocardium**, is the cardiac muscle. The inner layer, the **endocardium**, is connective tissue lined with endothelium, which separates the myocardium from the blood in the chambers.

In the ventricles the muscle fibers do not run in one direction. They wind around the chambers in spiraling layers from base to apex, and their angle changes through the thickness of the wall. When they shorten, the ventricle does not just squeeze in from the sides. It wrings, like a towel being twisted, and pushes blood out toward the valves at the base.

### The cardiac myocyte

Cardiac myocytes are:

- **striated**, with sarcomeres just like skeletal muscle;
- **branched**, so each cell connects to several neighbors;
- joined end to end by **intercalated discs**;
- packed with **mitochondria**, which take up about 30% of the cell's volume. The heart never rests, so it depends on a steady supply of ATP from oxidative metabolism;
- usually **mononucleated**, with a single central nucleus (some cells have two).

Each cell is about 100 µm long, much shorter than a skeletal muscle fiber, which is one multinucleated cell that can run the length of the muscle.

### Sarcolemma and T-tubules

The sarcolemma, the myocyte's cell membrane, carries the transporters and channels that set the membrane potential. At each Z line it dips deep into the cell as a **T-tubule** (transverse tubule). The inside of a T-tubule is extracellular space: it is open to the fluid outside the cell, and its lining of negatively charged polysaccharides binds Ca^2+^, so the T-tubules hold a supply of extracellular Ca^2+^ right next to the channels that let it in. Because the T-tubules carry the membrane deep into the cell, an action potential on the surface reaches every myofibril almost at once.

Each T-tubule runs right next to the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR). In cardiac muscle a T-tubule pairs with one SR cisterna, a **dyad** (@fig-cardiac-muscle-dyad-triad). Skeletal muscle has **triads**: one T-tubule flanked by two SR cisternae. Cardiac T-tubules are also wider, there is one per sarcomere instead of two, and the SR is less extensive than in skeletal muscle. The slides write "diads"; the course term is dyad.

![Triad and dyad. (A) In skeletal muscle, T-tubules (blue) enter at the junctions of the A and I bands, two per sarcomere, and each has an SR cisterna (purple) on both sides. (B) In cardiac muscle, a wider T-tubule enters at each Z line and pairs with a single SR cisterna. Thin purple lines are the SR network running between cisternae. Schematic. Course figure.](figures/cardiac-muscle/dyad-triad.svg){#fig-cardiac-muscle-dyad-triad}

### The sarcoplasmic reticulum

The SR is the cell's main store of Ca^2+^ for contraction. Three proteins in its membrane matter here:

- the **ryanodine receptor** (RyR2 in the heart), a Ca^2+^ release channel. It senses Ca^2+^ in the cytosol, and when Ca^2+^ rises near it, it opens and releases SR Ca^2+^;
- **SERCA** (sarco/endoplasmic reticulum Ca^2+^-ATPase), a pump that uses ATP to move Ca^2+^ from the cytosol back into the SR;
- **phospholamban** (PLB), a small protein that regulates SERCA. Unphosphorylated, it holds SERCA back. When it is phosphorylated, the brake comes off and SERCA pumps faster.

Epinephrine and norepinephrine, acting through β~1~ receptors, raise cAMP and activate protein kinase A (PKA), which phosphorylates phospholamban. SERCA speeds up and Ca^2+^ uptake into the SR increases. You need only the result, not the steps of the cascade. The section on unique properties shows why that makes the heart beat more strongly.

::: {.callout-note title="If you are comparing with the slides"}
The SR slide and the peer-educator notes say that phospholamban "is unique to cardiac muscle." Phospholamban is the main regulator of SERCA in the heart, but it is also found in slow-twitch (type I) skeletal muscle and in smooth muscle. What matters for this course is that β~1~-adrenergic phosphorylation of phospholamban speeds Ca^2+^ uptake in the heart. This is errata entry 3.

The notes also say the SR "holds a large store of Ca^2+^ used for depolarization." SR Ca^2+^ is used for contraction, not depolarization. The myocyte depolarizes because Na^+^ enters, and its plateau comes from Ca^2+^ entering across the sarcolemma through L-type channels. Releasing SR Ca^2+^ is the step that links the action potential to contraction. This is errata entry 19.
:::

### The sarcomere and troponin

The cardiac sarcomere has the same parts as the skeletal sarcomere: Z lines anchoring the thin (actin) filaments, an M line in the middle anchoring the thick (myosin) filaments, the light I band (thin filaments only), the dark A band (the full length of the thick filaments), and the H zone in the middle of the A band (thick filaments only), which narrows as the muscle shortens. The slides label it the H band. The details are in [Skeletal Muscle](skeletal-muscle.qmd).

Regulation is on the thin filament, as in skeletal muscle. Tropomyosin lies along the actin and covers the myosin-binding sites. The troponin complex sits on tropomyosin: troponin C binds Ca^2+^, troponin I inhibits actin-myosin binding, and troponin T anchors the complex to tropomyosin. When Ca^2+^ binds troponin C, the complex changes shape, tropomyosin moves, the binding sites are exposed, and cross-bridges form.

Cardiac troponin C has **one regulatory Ca^2+^-binding site**, and skeletal troponin C has two. Both also have two structural sites that bind Ca^2+^ or Mg^2+^, so in all cardiac troponin C has three sites and skeletal has four. The single regulatory site is the one that switches contraction on.

::: {.callout-note title="If you are comparing with the slides"}
The sarcomere slide and the peer-educator notes say "Troponin C only has 1 calcium binding site (Skeletal muscle has 4)." That compares cardiac regulatory sites (one) with skeletal total sites (four). Compared like with like, cardiac troponin C has one regulatory site and skeletal has two, and cardiac has three sites in all and skeletal four. This is errata entry 4.
:::

**A clinical correlation.** Cardiac troponin I and troponin T are cardiac-specific isoforms, different enough from the skeletal forms that blood tests can tell them apart. When cardiac myocytes are injured, as in a myocardial infarction, troponin leaks out of the dying cells and its level in the blood rises. That is why a troponin level is drawn in a patient with chest pain.

### Intercalated discs

Where two myocytes meet end to end, their membranes form an intercalated disc. It runs in steps (@fig-cardiac-muscle-intercalated-disc). The *transverse* parts of each step run across the long axis of the cells, and the myofibrils end there. The *longitudinal* parts run along the long axis. Each part holds different junctions.

![An intercalated disc between two cardiac myocytes. Myofibrils (pink bands; gray lines are Z lines) end at the transverse parts of the disc, where adherens junctions (green) anchor them and desmosomes (gold) rivet the membranes together. Gap junctions (blue) lie in the longitudinal parts. Schematic. Course figure, after the lecture's electron micrographs.](figures/cardiac-muscle/intercalated-disc.svg){#fig-cardiac-muscle-intercalated-disc}

**Gap junctions (longitudinal regions): communication.** Each gap junction channel is made of 12 connexin proteins, six from each cell. Each set of six forms a half-channel, and the two halves line up across the narrow gap between the cells to make a channel connecting the two cytoplasms. Ions and small molecules flow freely through it. That is why the gap junction matters: when one myocyte depolarizes, current flows through the gap junctions into its neighbors and depolarizes them. The action potential spreads from cell to cell without any nerve, and the whole myocardium contracts as a coordinated unit, a *functional syncytium*.

**Adherens junctions (transverse regions): the zipper.** Cadherins span the gap between the cells. Inside each cell, α-catenin and β-catenin link the cadherins to the actin of the cytoskeleton, and the myofibrils attach here. Force generated in one cell's sarcomeres is passed straight to the next cell.

**Desmosomes (transverse regions): the rivet.** The transmembrane proteins desmoglein and desmocollin bind across the gap. Inside the cell, desmoplakin connects them to desmin, an intermediate filament. Desmosomes hold the cells firmly together so they do not pull apart when the heart contracts.

## Conduction system and autorhythmicity

The heart starts its own beat. Specialized cardiac cells generate the impulse and carry it through the heart in order:

1. **Sinoatrial (SA) node**, in the right atrium, the heart's pacemaker. It fires fastest, so it sets the rate.
2. **Internodal pathways** through the atria, and **Bachmann's bundle**, which carries the impulse to the left atrium.
3. **Atrioventricular (AV) node**, which delays the impulse so the atria finish contracting before the ventricles start.
4. **Bundle of His**.
5. **Left and right bundle branches** and the **Purkinje fibers**, which spread the impulse quickly through the ventricular walls.

These conductive cells are specialized myocytes, not nerves. They contain little actin and myosin, so they contract weakly or not at all. They are also anatomically isolated from the surrounding working myocytes: the Purkinje fibers, for example, run in bundles wrapped in connective tissue, and they connect to ordinary myocytes only at their ends.

Pacemaker cells and ordinary ventricular myocytes have different action potentials (@fig-cardiac-muscle-action-potentials). A ventricular myocyte sits at a stable resting potential of about −90 mV until a neighbor depolarizes it. Its fast-response action potential rises sharply (phase 0), dips briefly (phase 1), holds a long plateau near 0 mV (phase 2), repolarizes (phase 3) and returns to rest (phase 4). A pacemaker cell has no stable resting potential. Its slow-response action potential starts from a maximum diastolic potential of about −60 mV and drifts upward in phase 4 until it reaches threshold, then rises slowly (phase 0) and repolarizes (phase 3).

Autonomic nerves change heart rate by changing that phase 4 drift. Sympathetic stimulation (norepinephrine at β~1~ receptors) steepens it, so threshold comes sooner and the rate rises. Parasympathetic stimulation (acetylcholine at M~2~ receptors) does two things at once: it opens K^+^ channels, so each cycle starts from a more negative potential, and it lowers cAMP, so the slope flattens. Both lengthen the time to threshold and slow the heart. The lecture's figure shows only the flatter slope; both effects happen together, as [Autonomic and Extrinsic Control](../cardiovascular/ans-extrinsic-control.qmd) explains.

![Cardiac action potentials. (A) A pacemaker cell in the SA node has a slow-response action potential with spontaneous phase 4 depolarization. Sympathetic stimulation (maroon) steepens phase 4 and the cell reaches threshold sooner. Parasympathetic stimulation (blue) starts phase 4 from a more negative potential and flattens its slope, so the cell reaches threshold later. (B) A ventricular myocyte has a fast-response action potential with phases 0 to 4. The absolute (effective) refractory period lasts through the plateau and about midway through phase 3, and the relative refractory period covers the rest of phase 3. Schematic. Course figure.](figures/cardiac-muscle/action-potentials.svg){#fig-cardiac-muscle-action-potentials}

The ionic currents behind each phase are the subject of [EKG I: Ionic Basis](../cardiovascular/ecg-ionic-basis.qmd).

::: {.callout-warning title="A common mistake"}
The upstroke of a slow-response action potential, in the SA and AV nodes, is carried by Ca^2+^ through L-type channels, not by Na^+^. That is why L-type Ca^2+^ channel blockers slow conduction through the AV node. What this means for other drugs is in [Membrane Potentials and Excitable Cells](excitable-cells.qmd) and [EKG I: Ionic Basis](../cardiovascular/ecg-ionic-basis.qmd).
:::

The absolute (effective) refractory period of a ventricular myocyte lasts through the plateau and about midway through phase 3, almost as long as the contraction itself. The relative refractory period covers the rest of phase 3. The cell cannot fire again until it has largely relaxed, so the heart cannot be tetanized the way skeletal muscle can.

## Excitation-contraction coupling

Excitation-contraction coupling is the chain of steps that turns the action potential into contraction. In cardiac muscle it runs in six steps (@fig-cardiac-muscle-calcium-cycle).

1. **The action potential arrives.** It starts in the SA node, travels through the conduction system to the myocytes, and spreads from cell to cell through gap junctions. In each cell it runs down the T-tubules, deep into the cell, close to the SR.
2. **L-type Ca^2+^ channels open.** Depolarization of the T-tubule membrane opens voltage-gated L-type Ca^2+^ channels, and Ca^2+^ flows into the cell from the extracellular fluid in the T-tubule. This entry is the plateau current.
3. **Ca^2+^ activates the ryanodine receptor.** The incoming Ca^2+^ diffuses across the narrow gap of the dyad and binds RyR2 on the SR.
4. **The SR releases a large amount of Ca^2+^.** RyR2 opens and releases far more Ca^2+^ from the SR into the cytosol than came in through the L-type channels. A small trigger releases a large store: *Ca^2+^-induced Ca^2+^ release*.
5. **Ca^2+^ binds troponin C.** The troponin complex changes shape, tropomyosin moves off the myosin-binding sites on actin, and cross-bridges cycle. The sarcomeres shorten. The cross-bridge cycle is the one in [Skeletal Muscle](skeletal-muscle.qmd).
6. **Ca^2+^ is removed and the myocyte relaxes.** About 70% of the Ca^2+^ is pumped back into the SR by SERCA, under the control of phospholamban. NCX, the Na^+^/Ca^2+^ exchanger, removes most of the rest (about 28%) from the cell, bringing three Na^+^ in for each Ca^2+^ it moves out. The last 2% or so leaves through the sarcolemmal Ca^2+^-ATPase and the mitochondria (the slide shows it going to the mitochondria). As Ca^2+^ leaves troponin C, tropomyosin covers the binding sites again.

![Ca^2+^ handling in a ventricular myocyte. (1) The action potential depolarizes the sarcolemma and T-tubule. (2) L-type Ca^2+^ channels in the T-tubule let a small amount of Ca^2+^ in. (3) That Ca^2+^ opens RyR2 on the SR. (4) The SR releases a large amount of Ca^2+^. (5) Ca^2+^ binds troponin C and the myofilaments contract. (6) Ca^2+^ is removed: about 70% back into the SR by SERCA (regulated by phospholamban, PLB), 28% out of the cell by NCX, and about 2% by the sarcolemmal Ca^2+^ pump and the mitochondria. The Na^+^/K^+^ pump keeps up the Na^+^ gradient that drives NCX. Course figure, after the lecture's diagram.](figures/cardiac-muscle/calcium-cycle.svg){#fig-cardiac-muscle-calcium-cycle}

Two consequences follow from these numbers. First, most of the Ca^2+^ that activates the myofilaments comes from the SR, not from outside the cell. Extracellular Ca^2+^ is still essential: without the trigger there is no release, and a cardiac myocyte will not contract in Ca^2+^-free solution. Second, in a steady state, whatever Ca^2+^ enters through the L-type channels each beat has to leave the cell again, mostly through NCX. What SERCA takes back into the SR is available for the next beat.

**How this differs from skeletal muscle.** In skeletal muscle, the voltage sensor in the T-tubule (the dihydropyridine, or DHP, receptor) is mechanically linked to the ryanodine receptor (RyR1) and opens it directly by changing shape. No Ca^2+^ has to enter from outside, and skeletal muscle keeps contracting in Ca^2+^-free solution. In cardiac muscle the L-type Ca^2+^ channel is the same family of protein, but it is not physically coupled to RyR2. It works by letting Ca^2+^ in, and that Ca^2+^ opens RyR2.

## Unique properties

### Force depends on sarcomere length

As in skeletal muscle, the force a cardiac myocyte develops depends on how long its sarcomeres are when it starts to contract. In skeletal muscle, force is greatest at the length where thin and thick filaments overlap best (about 2.0 to 2.2 µm) and falls off as the sarcomere is shortened or stretched away from that length. Cardiac muscle works over a much narrower window (@fig-cardiac-muscle-length-tension). Its active force rises steeply as the sarcomere is stretched from about 1.8 to about 2.3 µm, and its passive tension (the force needed to stretch the resting muscle) rises steeply above about 2.2 µm. The heart normally works on the rising limb of its length-tension curve.

![Length-tension curve of cardiac muscle. Solid line, active tension; dashed line, passive tension of resting muscle. Active force rises steeply between about 1.8 and 2.3 µm, and passive tension rises so steeply above about 2.2 µm that the sarcomeres in an intact heart are rarely stretched much farther. The curve is for the Ca^2+^ level of a normal beat. For the skeletal muscle curve, see the [Skeletal Muscle](skeletal-muscle.qmd) chapter. Schematic. Course figure, after the lecture's slide.](figures/cardiac-muscle/length-tension.svg){#fig-cardiac-muscle-length-tension}

::: {.callout-note title="If you are comparing with the slides"}
The length-tension slide and the peer-educator notes say that cardiac sarcomeres are shorter than skeletal sarcomeres, which "makes for narrower window of optimal contraction." The thick filaments are the same length in both, and the sarcomere lengths overlap. The window is narrow mainly because resting cardiac muscle is so stiff: its giant elastic protein (titin) and its extracellular matrix resist stretch, so passive tension climbs steeply above about 2.2 µm and keeps the sarcomeres near the top of their working range even when the heart is very full. The rising limb is also steeper in heart muscle, because at the Ca^2+^ level of a normal beat a shorter sarcomere is less sensitive to Ca^2+^ (see the Frank-Starling mechanism below). The practical point is the same either way: the heart works over a narrow range of sarcomere lengths, on the rising part of its curve.

The slide's cardiac curve also peaks near 2.4 µm and then falls steeply. In the intact heart, passive stiffness keeps sarcomeres from going much past 2.2 to 2.3 µm, so that falling limb is rarely reached, and the figure here draws only the range the heart uses. What matters is the shape: the heart works on the rising limb, over a narrow range, while skeletal muscle works over a broader range around its 2.0 to 2.2 µm peak.
:::

### The Frank-Starling mechanism

The more the ventricle fills in diastole, the more its sarcomeres are stretched, and the more forcefully it contracts. Stroke volume rises with end-diastolic volume. This is the *Frank-Starling mechanism*, and it lets the heart pump out whatever returns to it, beat by beat, without any nerve or hormone.

Stretch raises force in two ways. Lengthening the sarcomere toward about 2.2 µm improves the overlap of thin and thick filaments. Stretch also makes the myofilaments more sensitive to Ca^2+^: at a longer sarcomere length, the same Ca^2+^ concentration produces more force (@fig-cardiac-muscle-frank-starling A). In the heart the second effect is thought to be the larger one.

![(A) Force developed by cardiac muscle at different Ca^2+^ concentrations, at a short and a stretched sarcomere length. pCa is −log[Ca^2+^], so Ca^2+^ concentration rises to the right. At the longer length the curve shifts left: the same Ca^2+^ gives more force. Lengths as on the lecture's slide, measured in isolated heart muscle, which can be stretched farther than sarcomeres in an intact heart. (B) Frank-Starling curves. Moving from point 1 to point 2, more filling stretches the muscle and stroke volume rises along the same curve, with contractility unchanged. Moving from point 1 to point 3, contractility rises (for example with sympathetic stimulation) and the heart ejects more at the same end-diastolic volume, on a higher curve. A fall in contractility moves the heart to a lower curve. Schematic values. Course figure, after the lecture's slides.](figures/cardiac-muscle/frank-starling.svg){#fig-cardiac-muscle-frank-starling}

Keep the two kinds of change apart (@fig-cardiac-muscle-frank-starling B). More filling moves the heart *along* its Frank-Starling curve: force and stroke volume rise, and contractility does not change. A change in contractility moves the heart *to a different curve*: more (or less) force at the same end-diastolic volume. At very high filling volumes the curve flattens, so more filling adds little stroke volume. The [Cardiac Pump](../cardiovascular/cardiac-pump.qmd) chapter shows the same distinction on the pressure-volume loop, where more filling moves the beat along the same end-systolic pressure-volume line and greater contractility makes the line steeper.

::: {.callout-note title="If you are comparing with the slides"}
The Frank-Starling slides say "Starling Curve maps contractility with stretch" and "Increased filling and stretch can lead to decreased contractility." Stretch raises the *force of contraction* and the stroke volume, not contractility: more filling moves the heart along the same Frank-Starling curve. At very high filling the curve flattens, so more filling adds little stroke volume. That flattening is not a fall in contractility. Contractility changes only when the state of the muscle changes, and then the heart moves to a higher or lower curve.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="A common mistake"}
"Stretching the ventricle increases its contractility" is wrong. Stretch increases the *force* of contraction through the Frank-Starling mechanism, and contractility is unchanged: the heart stays on the same curve.
:::

### Force depends on Ca^2+^

A cardiac myocyte will not contract without Ca^2+^, and the force it develops depends on how much Ca^2+^ reaches the myofilaments. In skeletal muscle a single twitch is brief and submaximal, and the body grades force by recruiting more motor units and by firing them faster, so that Ca^2+^ stays high (summation and tetanus). In the heart every cell contracts on every beat, and none can be tetanized, so the heart grades force partly by length (Frank-Starling) and partly by how much Ca^2+^ each beat releases. At normal levels the Ca^2+^ released in a beat fills only part of the troponin C sites, which leaves room for more.

This is where phospholamban comes back. Epinephrine and norepinephrine, through β~1~ receptors and PKA, phosphorylate phospholamban. SERCA pumps faster, the SR takes up more Ca^2+^ and holds a larger store, and the next action potential releases more Ca^2+^. More Ca^2+^ on troponin C means a stronger contraction: contractility rises. Faster Ca^2+^ uptake also makes the myocyte relax faster, which helps the ventricle fill when heart rate is high. Phosphorylation of phospholamban is one way adrenergic signaling increases cardiac contractility.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Background: other PKA targets"}
The lecture's diagram of the β-adrenergic cascade shows that PKA also phosphorylates the L-type Ca^2+^ channel (more Ca^2+^ enters each beat), the ryanodine receptor, and troponin I (Ca^2+^ comes off troponin C faster, so relaxation speeds up). Acetylcholine at M~2~ receptors, through Gi, lowers cAMP and opposes these effects. The lecture says you do not need to memorize this part of the cascade.
:::

## Summary

| Feature | Skeletal muscle | Cardiac muscle | Smooth muscle |
|---|---|---|---|
| Control | Voluntary (somatic motor neurons) | Involuntary (intrinsic pacemaker, modulated by the autonomic nervous system) | Involuntary (autonomic, hormonal, stretch, NO) |
| Cells | Long, multinucleated fibers | Short, branched, usually one nucleus, joined by intercalated discs | Small, fusiform, one nucleus |
| Striations | Yes (sarcomeres) | Yes (sarcomeres) | No (dense bodies) |
| Membrane system | T-tubules and triads | Wider T-tubules and dyads | Caveolae, sparse SR |
| How the SR is triggered | DHP receptor mechanically coupled to RyR1 | Ca^2+^ entry through L-type channels opens RyR2 (Ca^2+^-induced Ca^2+^ release) | Ca^2+^ entry and IP~3~ |
| Needs extracellular Ca^2+^ to contract | No | Yes | Yes, for sustained contraction |
| Ca^2+^ sensor | Troponin C | Troponin C | Calmodulin, which activates MLCK |
| Electrical coupling | None between fibers; each fiber has its own neuromuscular junction | Gap junctions in intercalated discs | Gap junctions in single-unit muscle |
| Can be tetanized | Yes | No (long refractory period) | Sustained contraction and latch |
| Range of working lengths | Broad, optimum about 2.0 to 2.2 µm | Narrow, on the rising limb | Wide; the optimum moves with adaptation |
| Can divide | No | No | Yes |

Stretch and Ca^2+^ handling return in [The Cardiac Pump](../cardiovascular/cardiac-pump.qmd) and [Control of Cardiac Output](../cardiovascular/control-of-co.qmd): stretch is how the heart responds to filling, and Ca^2+^ handling is the main thing contractility changes.

## Check your understanding

1. A drug blocks SERCA in a ventricular myocyte. Predict what happens to relaxation, and to the force of the beats that follow.

    <details><summary>Answer</summary>

    Relaxation slows, because the main route for clearing Ca^2+^ from the cytosol (about 70%) is gone and NCX has to do most of the work. Beat by beat the SR store runs down, because Ca^2+^ released from the SR is no longer pumped back. Less Ca^2+^ is released with each action potential, so less binds troponin C and force falls.

    </details>

2. A drug blocks the gap junctions between ventricular myocytes. What happens to the spread of excitation, and why does it matter for pumping?

    <details><summary>Answer</summary>

    The action potential can no longer pass from cell to cell through the gap junctions, so excitation spreads slowly or not at all. The myocytes stop contracting together as a functional syncytium, and the ventricle cannot squeeze its blood out in one coordinated contraction.

    </details>

3. During exercise the heart rate rises and the time between beats shrinks. How does β~1~ stimulation make each beat relax faster? Name the proteins PKA acts on and the pump involved, and say why faster relaxation matters at a high heart rate.

    <details><summary>Answer</summary>

    β~1~ receptors raise cAMP and activate PKA. PKA phosphorylates phospholamban, which takes its brake off SERCA, so SERCA pumps Ca^2+^ back into the SR faster. PKA also phosphorylates troponin I, so Ca^2+^ comes off troponin C sooner. Cytosolic Ca^2+^ falls faster, cross-bridges detach sooner, and the myocyte relaxes earlier in each cycle. The speed of relaxation is lusitropy, a property separate from contractility. At a high heart rate the ventricle has little time between beats to fill, and relaxing early leaves more of that time for filling.

    </details>

4. On the Frank-Starling curves in @fig-cardiac-muscle-frank-starling B, a heart can reach the same larger stroke volume by moving from point 1 to point 2 or from point 1 to point 3. What is different about the sarcomeres in the two cases, and which one involves a change in contractility?

    <details><summary>Answer</summary>

    From 1 to 2, the heart fills more, so its sarcomeres start each beat longer. That raises force through better filament overlap and greater Ca^2+^ sensitivity, with no change in contractility: the heart stays on the same curve. From 1 to 3, sarcomere length at the start of the beat is the same, but more Ca^2+^ is released and bound each beat (for example after β~1~ stimulation phosphorylates phospholamban). The heart develops more force at the same length, which is what a rise in contractility means, so it moves to a higher curve.

    </details>

5. Of the Ca^2+^ that activates contraction in each beat, most is removed by SERCA and about 28% by NCX. Why must the NCX fraction roughly match the Ca^2+^ that entered through the L-type channels?

    <details><summary>Answer</summary>

    In a steady state the cell cannot gain or lose Ca^2+^ from beat to beat. Ca^2+^ that came in from outside through the L-type channels has to go back out, and NCX is the main route out. Ca^2+^ taken back up by SERCA stays inside, in the SR, ready for the next beat.

    </details>

6. A ventricular myocyte's action potential lasts 250 ms and its twitch 300 ms. A second stimulus arrives either 100 ms or 320 ms after the first upstroke. Which timing fires a second action potential, and does the force of the second beat add to the first?

    <details><summary>Answer</summary>

    At 100 ms the cell is in its plateau, inside the absolute refractory period, so the stimulus fires nothing and the first twitch runs its course unchanged. At 320 ms the action potential is over and the twitch has ended, so the stimulus fires a new action potential and a new twitch. That twitch starts from a relaxed muscle, and its force does not add to the first. The cell can fire again only once it has largely relaxed, so cardiac twitches do not summate.

    </details>
